title: 'Bad time to troll': Binance cofounder Changpeng Zhao asks Elon Musk for 'respect' after post about bitcoin hack
description: Changpeng Zhao, co-founder of Binance Holdings Ltd., during the Bitcoin Asia conference in Hong Kong, China, on Thursday, Aug. 27, 2026. Chan Long Hei
body: Changpeng Zhao, co-founder of Binance Holdings Ltd., during the Bitcoin Asia conference in Hong Kong, China, on Thursday, Aug. 27, 2026. Chan Long Hei | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe cofounder and former CEO of Binance asked Elon Musk not to "troll" the company on Friday and instead "show some support" after the SpaceX CEO appeared to mock the embattled cryptocurrency exchange in a series of social media posts.After learning the world's largest crypto exchange had been hit by a $6.3 billion hack late Thursday, Musk posted several emojis, ranging from laughing to grimacing, on X.In response, Changpeng Zhao reminded the SpaceX and Tesla CEO of Binance's equity stake in Musk's businesses.Binance’s SpaceX stake, which stems from an earlier investment in what was then-Twitter, is worth more than $1 billion, Zhao said. That's a tiny fraction of SpaceX's roughly $2 trillion valuation."Elon, have a lot of respect for you, but bad time to troll. Please stop," Zhao wrote. "Our SPCX shares (from our $500m investment in your Twitter takeover) are worth more than a billion. Would appreciate if you show a little support. Thanks!"It's not the first time the pair has sparred online. In Nov. 2021, Binance suspended Dogecoin withdrawals because of a wallet glitch, a measure Musk called "shady". In reply, Zhao highlighted a major Tesla recall of almost 12,000 U.S. vehicles due to software glitches and hardware issues. Binance froze all withdrawals and deposits after the hack, which investigators suspect to be the work of North Korean state-sponsored hacking unit TraderTraitor. It has since restored deposits.Around $3 billion in cryptocurrency assets have been frozen so far.

title: Russian strikes plunge Ukrainian city into blackout as Zelenskyy warns of more missile attacks
description: LONDON, ENGLAND - OCTOBER 14: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky reacts during a meeting with Britain's Prime Minister Andy Burnham at 10 Downing
body: LONDON, ENGLAND - OCTOBER 14: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky reacts during a meeting with Britain's Prime Minister Andy Burnham at 10 Downing Street on October 14, 2026 in London, England. (Photo by Henry Nicholls-WPA Pool/Getty Images)Wpa Pool | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesRussia and Ukraine traded strikes on each other's energy infrastructure overnight as the Ukrainian city of Dnipro saw a near-total blackout and an oil refinery in western Russia was engulfed in flames after a drone attack.Emergency power cuts came into force in Dnipro and Dnipropetrovsk Oblast early Friday after damage from Russian attacks, according to Ukrainian private energy company DTEK. More than 350,000 people were left without power and work is ongoing to restore supply, Oleksandr Hanzha, the head of the military administration in the region, said in a Telegram post.SHAKHTARSKE, UKRAINE - OCTOBER 27: People walk near damaged cars after a Russian drone strike on October 27, 2026 in Shakhtarske, Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, Ukraine. At least four apartment buildings and about a dozen cars were damaged because of a Russian attack on Shakhtarske on the evening of October 26. According to residents, one of the drones struck an apartment on the second floor of a multi-story building. (Photo by Yurii Tynnyi/Suspilne Ukraine/JSC "UA:PBC"/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images)Global Images Ukraine | Global Images Ukraine | Getty ImagesAn oil refinery in the Russian city of Novokuibyshevsk in Samara Oblast that produced jet fuel for the Russian armed forces was set on fire after being hit by a Ukrainian drone.Late Thursday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces had destroyed two Russian Su-34 fighter jets and struck an Iskander missile launcher. He also warned that Russia was preparing further high-speed missile attacks and urged Ukraine's allies to urgently supply more air defense interceptors, particularly for Patriot systems."We now have intel about the Russians preparing new ballistic missile attacks," Zelenskyy said in an evening address from Kyiv. "We need the capabilities to shoot down this Russian evil and are awaiting the decisions," he added, referring to anti-ballistic defense capabilities provided by allies.Ukraine is facing an acute shortage of interceptors to shoot down incoming Russian ballistic missiles. Early Thursday, at least 14 people were killed in an attack on a Ukrainian rail platform in Dnipro, while at least six more people died in additional strikes throughout the day, according to officials. The attacks came as a six-day local ceasefire in Kherson in southern Ukraine appeared to hold for a third day, raising cautious optimism that a broader truce may be possible. While attempts at a peace deal have so far been unsuccessful, a new round of U.S.-brokered peace negotiations is expected next month in Abu Dhabi. Both sides have emphasized the need for security guarantees.Tensions have run high between Zelenskyy and President Donald Trump in recent weeks, amid a series of moves by the Trump administration that appeared to favor Russia, including easing of economic sanctions.Reuters reported Friday that the Pentagon has told NATO allies to tone down public criticism of Russia, citing four people familiar with the matter.Trump has also accused Ukraine of raising fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3 with attacks on Russian energy facilities.An "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine announced by Trump on Oct. 11 failed to yield any meaningful outcome.

title: Fed officials are already saying they’ll need to get back to hiking rates
description: Alberto Musalem, President and CEO of the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, speaks to the Economic Club of New York, in New York City, U.S., Feb. 20,
body: Alberto Musalem, President and CEO of the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, speaks to the Economic Club of New York, in New York City, U.S., Feb. 20, 2025.Brendan McDermid | ReutersSt. Louis Federal Reserve President Alberto Musalem said Friday that higher interest rates will be needed in the near future to rein in inflation."I judge that additional firming of monetary policy will be necessary, and soon," Musalem said in prepared remarks for the Shadow Open Market Committee, a gathering of economists focused on the central bank.Musalem's comments offer the first morsels of insight into what leaders at the Fed see next following Wednesday's decision to hold interest rates steady. It will also bolster the view among investors that the Fed will return to hiking rates at its next meeting in December. Fed funds futures traders are pricing in a roughly 76% likelihood of the Fed lifting rates by a quarter percentage point at that gathering, according to CME's FedWatch tool."Incremental adjustments made earlier are usually less disruptive than larger and abrupt actions taken later," Musalem said. "Moving sooner in smaller steps while inflation expectations are anchored has a better chance of succeeding without adverse impact on the labor market or economic growth."Musalem broadly spoke positively about the state of the U.S. economy, which he described as "resilient." He pointed to Thursday's data on U.S. GDP, which showed a stronger-than-expected growth rate of 3.4%.He said there are several factors boosting the economy, including the artificial-intelligence buildout and financial conditions that "remain accommodative."Musalem said the labor market has been "remarkably stable and balanced." The unemployment rate of 4.2% sits at the median of long-run projections by participants in the Federal Open Market Committee, the group tasked with setting interest rates, he noted. Musalem is not a voting member of the FOMC this year, and isn't expected to have a vote until 2028.But Musalem warned that inflation is "too high," citing the personal consumption expenditures price index released Thursday that showed annual inflation above 3%. In the question-and-answer portion of the event, Musalem said he's watching core inflation closely, and is on alert for any indications that current inflationary pressures are broadening out.Fed officials have been closely monitoring inflation expectations among consumers and investors to ensure they don't get too far above the central bank's long-term target of 2%.He said there's a likely scenario where inflation remains above 2% into the future unless the Fed adjusts monetary policy."The best that monetary policy can do now for employment and economic growth is to restore  price stability in a timely manner," Musalem said. "The short-run economic costs of reducing inflation are less when the central bank acts before inflation has become entrenched and is expected to persist."

schema.headline: Fed officials are already saying they’ll need to get back to hiking rates

title: Class action lawsuit blames Trump officials for student loan forgiveness delays
description: Linda McMahon, US education secretary, speaks during a roundtable on education at the Department of Justice (DOJ) in Washington, DC, US, on Thursday,
body: Linda McMahon, US education secretary, speaks during a roundtable on education at the Department of Justice (DOJ) in Washington, DC, US, on Thursday, June 11, 2026. Al Drago | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe American Federation of Teachers sued the Trump administration Friday, alleging it unlawfully blocked student loan forgiveness for tens of thousands of borrowers who qualify.The plaintiffs argue in their lawsuit, Weingarten v. McMahon, filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, that U.S. Department of Education Secretary Linda McMahon has mismanaged the popular Public Service Loan Forgiveness program by incorrectly counting borrower's payment timelines and not awarding people credit for time served. PSLF, which President George W. Bush signed into law in 2007, allows certain not-for-profit and government employees to have their federal student loans canceled after 120 payments, generally paid over 10 years. The Biden administration later adapted the program, making it easier to qualify for it and clearing the way for more than 1 million borrowers to have already had their loans forgiven under the program. "Secretary McMahon has flagrantly ignored her responsibility to help teachers, nurses and first responders," said AFT President Randi Weingarten, the lead plaintiff, in a statement. The other plaintiffs include AFT members and public service workers. The AFT is a teacher's union representing some 1.8 million members. "This lawsuit demands that McMahon stop stalling and do her job," Weingarten said. Read more CNBC personal finance coverageIf Elon Musk gifts SpaceX stock through Trump Accounts, it will come with a catchRoth conversions aren't for everyone. When the 'juice' isn't worth it: Top advisorThe affordability crisis isn't hitting all voters equally. Here's whyMidterm elections: How affordability and the economy could affect voters' decisionsCNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 rankedCNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026The lawsuit accuses Trump officials of denying borrowers relief under the Biden administration-era PSLF Buyback program. That opportunity allows borrowers who've hit 120 months of qualifying employment to submit a request to the Education Department to retroactively pay for any months they missed because of a forbearance or deferment. Buyback applications have piled up under the Trump administration, with 88,000 borrowers still waiting for a decision as of the spring, according to a court filing. The borrowers bringing the lawsuit also say the U.S. Department of Education unfairly lowered their qualifying payment counts out of the blue earlier this year, prolonging borrowers' student loan forgiveness timeline. "The Department of Education has ripped away the loan forgiveness credit I earned without any explanation," said Elizabeth Schoepflin, a speech-language pathologist and co-plaintiff from New York, in a statement. "Every month this drags on is another payment I shouldn't have to make." An Education Department spokesperson defended the PSLF program changes, saying the agency is correcting "coding errors" made by the Biden administration. "These errors resulted in inaccurate payment counts for some borrowers," the spokesperson wrote to CNBC in an email. "The Department remains committed to ensuring that every qualifying payment is properly credited to a borrower's account."

title: The AI investing story had a rough week. It may be time to take profits while you still can
description: Traders work on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York City, U.S., Oct. 30, 2026.  Brendan McDermid | ReutersMarket professionals
body: Traders work on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York City, U.S., Oct. 30, 2026.  Brendan McDermid | ReutersMarket professionals are sounding worried about the artificial intelligence trade after a big week of data points in the technology sector. Investors are focused on the scale of the AI build-out and whether returns are materializing fast enough to justify it.The overall stock bull market driven originally by the AI boom remains intact, with the S&P 500 just a few percent off a record. A rotation into non-AI stocks like Procter & Gamble and Berkshire Hathaway have stepped in to support the market. But AI-related shares are already in a bear market or teetering on one.It may be time to take some profits or hedge your risk.This week, frontier algorithm maker Anthropic's public filing document didn't contain much information on forthcoming revenues after the company reported a deceleration in sales from the second to the third quarter. At the same time, we learned from the Big Tech earnings reports that hyperscalers are pulling back on their capital expenditures, suggesting they see a terminal level of required computing power at some point in the future.We've reached the point where profits need to be showing up in force from AI to justify the buildout that's happened so far and is still to come, investors and traders say.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconGlobal X Artificial Intelligence & Technology ETF, YTDDoubts creeping in"You want to make sure that the reward is worth the risk," JJ Kinahan, SVP at Cboe Global Markets, told CNBC on Friday. "I think the reward will be [there], but it continues to be a lot of money up front."Kinahan said he thought the recent AI boom over the past few years was "in question." AI-linked Technology stocks were getting housed on Friday in a variety of sectors. Intel was down 25% on lackluster revenue guidance, Micron was down 5.5%, and Nvidia was down 4%. Hyperscalers were also getting clobbered, with Amazon down 2% and Google down another 1%. Google had its worst trading day ever on Thursday after reporting a drop in its core advertising sales revenues.Like traders, technology investors were also sounding down about the AI trade on Friday."I'm a little worried about the trade," Mike Khouw, YieldMax strategist, said. "I think we're probably going to get a little bit more chopping here."Accordingly, options specialists say they're seeing more people pursuing downside insurance."Historically, tech stocks have call skews. So people are more willing to buy greed [with] upside calls than they are to buy insurance downside puts. I've seen that reverse in the last three days," Dennis Davitt, CIO and co-founder of Millbank Dartmoor Portsmouth, said.There's another interesting signal coming from options, Davitt noted: While investors may be getting cold feet about the big tech companies associated with the AI trade writ large, they may also be gaining confidence about the commercial prospects of AI technology itself, specifically with new successful consumer agents, such as Meta's Muse."I think the ChatGPTs and the [other AI algorithms] of the world are actually taking over from the Amazons of the world as well as the Googles of the world," he said. "You see Muse of Facebook – If you look at options pricing in Muse, there's less fear priced in Meta than there is in Amazon."Longer-term confidence in AI could be a silver lining for the slip in bread-and-butter ad sales reported by Alphabet this week. The stock fell by more than 10% after reporting earnings on Wednesday.Google executive Philipp Schindler called attention to the growth of AI mode use at the company even as it still has lower monetization at this point."It's worth noting the strong growth in AI mode queries had an impact because of the lower monetization we are seeing in AI mode," he said Wednesday.Still, the shifts in usage and monetization matter less to the fate of the AI trade than overall productivity and profit. All that capex needs to produce a profit, propelled by boosted productivity from businesses using AI.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconiShares Semiconductor ETF, YTDMacroeconomic reflections about this from top investors over the past few weeks are sounding rather gloomy, though nobody is super about the specific timing."Maybe the markets will continue to kick the can down the road," Paul Tudor Jones, Tudor Investment Corporation founder, said earlier this month, contemplating the possibility of a "tipping point" and saying that the odds were 60-40 that "we're down that path.""[AI-related issuance as a share of GDP] is 50% more than railroads, triple that of highways, telecoms, the other big infrastructure buildouts in history. So that competition between AI buildout and sovereigns may take us to the tipping point," he added.Technical analyst Jonathan Krinsky at BTIG recommended fading the chip bounce earlier this month, making comparisons in the SOX semiconductor index to some major down-legs in its history.Investors were rotating away from the tech sector on Friday, with names like Coca-Cola, Walmart and Eli Lilly all up over 1%.

schema.headline: The AI investing story had a rough week. It may be time to take profits while you still can

title: Treasury Department announces new Series I bond rate of 5.51% for the next six months
description: Jetcityimage | Istock | Getty ImagesThe U.S. Department of the Treasury has announced new rates for Series I bonds. Newly purchased I bonds will pay 5
body: Jetcityimage | Istock | Getty ImagesThe U.S. Department of the Treasury has announced new rates for Series I bonds. Newly purchased I bonds will pay 5.51% annual interest from Nov. 1 through April 30, which is up from the 4.26% yield offered on purchases made through Oct. 31.The new rate includes a variable portion of 4.08% based on inflation data, and a fixed portion of 1.40%. The fixed rate is up from 0.90% announced in April, and the highest since 2006. Combined, the composite I bond rate is 5.51% after rounding, according to the Treasury. Read more CNBC personal finance coverageIf Elon Musk gifts SpaceX stock through Trump Accounts, it will come with a catchRoth conversions aren't for everyone. When the 'juice' isn't worth it: Top advisorThe affordability crisis isn't hitting all voters equally. Here's whyMidterm elections: How affordability and the economy could affect voters' decisionsCNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 rankedCNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026Amid the post-pandemic inflation peak, the I bond rate hit a record high of 9.62% in May 2022, and investors poured millions into the government-backed, nearly risk-free asset. As inflation cooled and I bond rates fell, many short-term investors redeemed I bonds. But investors could return as inflation pushes I bond rates back up, experts say. "I bonds are a lot more attractive at this point," said David Enna, founder of Tipswatch.com, a website that tracks Treasury inflation-protected securities, or TIPS, and I bond rates.  I bonds are a lot more attractive at this point.David EnnaFounder of Tipswatch.comThe consumer price index rose 3.7% in September 2026 from one year earlier, up from an annual pace of 3.4% in August, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported in October.In September, some higher inflation came from the Iran war, which pushed up gasoline and energy costs. President Donald Trump's tariffs, new artificial intelligence data centers and demand for travel have also added to rising prices, economists say. Consumers expect rising inflation to continue. In September, the one-year inflation outlook jumped to 3.9%, the highest in more than three years, according to a New York Fed survey released in early October. How I bond rates workI bond rates have a variable and fixed rate portion, which the Treasury adjusts every six months, in May and November. The variable rate is tied to inflation — using the consumer price index percentage change over six months — and stays the same for six months after you purchase, regardless of the Treasury's next update. Your fixed rate doesn't change after purchasing I bonds. The Treasury doesn't disclose how it calculates fixed-rate adjustments, making it harder to predict.Some experts believe the I bond fixed rate could be driven by real, or inflation-adjusted, yields from five-year TIPS, according to Ken Tumin, founder of DepositQuest.com, a blog that tracks I bond rates, among other deposit accounts. "There's some uncertainty there," Tumin said.   How the change affects current I bond investorsIf you currently own I bonds, rate updates follow a six-month timeline based on your original purchase date. After you own I bonds for six months, the variable yield changes to the next announced rate. But the fixed rate stays the same for the entire time you own the asset.For example, let's say you purchased I bonds in March when the variable rate was still 3.12% and the fixed rate was 0.9%. After six months, the variable portion would shift to 3.34%, announced in April 2026, but your fixed rate would remain 0.9%.You can earn I bond interest for up to 30 years, or less if you redeem the assets before that. However, you can't cash in I bonds for at least one year after you buy them. If you redeem within five years, you lose your last three months of interest.

schema.headline: Treasury Department announces new Series I bond rate of 5.51% for the next six months

title: Foxconn hopes to own 50% of the global AI server market within a couple years
description: The logo of multinational tech company Foxconn (also known as Hon Hai), which is a major manufacturer for Apple products, in Taipei, Taiwan, on April
body: The logo of multinational tech company Foxconn (also known as Hon Hai), which is a major manufacturer for Apple products, in Taipei, Taiwan, on April 16, 2025.Anadolu | Anadolu | Getty ImagesTaiwanese electronics giant Hon Hai Technology Group, or Foxconn, is looking to expand its artificial intelligence server market share and boost manufacturing in the United States, as demand for AI infrastructure shows little sign of slowing, Chairman Young Liu told CNBC.In an interview with CNBC's Christine Tan,  Liu said Foxconn's share of the global AI server market could reach 50% in a couple of years, potentially rising to around 45% next year."I think we can grow up to 50 percent," Liu said, referring to Foxconn's share of the global AI server market, which currently stands at around 40%.watch nowFormally known as Hon Hai Precision Industry, the company is best known as a major assembler of Apple's iPhones but has increasingly turned to AI infrastructure as a key growth driver.Liu expects AI infrastructure to account for 60% to 65% of Foxconn's revenue in the next three to five years, excluding edge AI devices — which run AI and machine learning algorithms directly on local hardware.Foxconn's production capacity was already fully booked for at least the next year and a half, Liu said, pointing to sustained demand for AI infrastructure.He said demand so far has come largely from AI model developers and cloud service providers, while governments and enterprises have yet to fully embrace the technology. AI demand remains “quite strong,” he added.U.S. manufacturing expansionFoxconn is looking to expand its U.S. manufacturing footprint, with Liu saying the company plans to move further up the supply chain to better serve the U.S. market."What we are going to do is we're going to move up the supply chain," he said, explaining that a broader manufacturing presence would allow Foxconn to respond more quickly to rising demand.However, higher manufacturing costs in the U.S. mean the company will initially focus on products with stronger margins, including AI server racks and data center equipment.Liu said greater production scale in the U.S. could eventually help lower manufacturing costs.The expansion comes as Foxconn seeks to strengthen its position across the AI infrastructure supply chain, from servers and racks to entire data centers and computing services.AI spending risksHowever, even as AI demand continues to grow, Liu emphasized the importance of managing investments carefully."Overinvestment will kill the company," he said, adding that Foxconn would keep a tight rein on spending as it expands its AI business.Liu said Foxconn could spend more than its planned $3 billion to $5 billion a year on AI, depending on how far it expands its vertical integration.Asked how the company would respond if major customers cut back on AI spending, Liu said weaker demand from one customer could be offset by growth elsewhere. However, an industry-wide slowdown would pose a much bigger challenge for Foxconn and the broader AI supply chain.

schema.headline: Foxconn hopes to own 50% of the global AI server market within a couple years

title: Chevron and Exxon hit all-time highs as refining profits soar in reaction to Iran and Ukraine wars
description: watch nowChevron and ExxonMobil on Friday reported profits that soared in the third quarter, as their U.S. refineries ramped up production to full cap
body: watch nowChevron and ExxonMobil on Friday reported profits that soared in the third quarter, as their U.S. refineries ramped up production to full capacity to take advantage of high diesel fuel prices.Chevron shares are up nearly 2% while Exxon is more than 1% higher. Both touched all-time highs Friday. The world is facing a fuel crisis as Ukraine, Iran and Houthi militants attack refineries in Russia and the Middle East, reducing global capacity by millions of barrels per day. Importers have increasingly turned to U.S. Gulf Coast refineries for diesel supplies as a consequence. ExxonMobil's profits doubled to $15.4 billion, or $3.72 a share, compared to $7.5 billion, or $1.76 a share, in the same period in 2025. When adjusted for one-time items, it posted earnings of $4.23 a share, soundly beating Wall Street's expectations. "Refining capacity is very tight today," Exxon CEO Darren Woods told CNBC in an interview. "Frankly, diesel is the key crunch point here because it is so critical to economic growth [with] very inelastic demand."U.S. diesel stood at a national average of $6.32 per gallon on Friday, an increase of more than 70% compared to the same period last year, according to AAA. Prices in the U.S. hit a record high in September. Chevron's net income surged nearly 200% to $9.9 billion, or $5.06 a share, compared to $3.5 billion, or $1.82 a share, in the same period last year. When adjusted for one-time items, it reported earnings of $5.28 per share, also beating the Street's expectations of $4.89. "The system is under stress," Chevron CEO Mike Wirth told CNBC in an interview. "We remain in an environment that is fairly fragile."Here's what Chevron and Exxon earned, compared with estimates from analysts polled by LSEG:Chevron earnings per share: $5.28 adjusted, vs. $4.89 expectedChevron revenue: $67.8 billion, vs. $61.6 billion expectedExxon earnings per share: $4.23 adjusted, vs. $4.08 expectedExxon revenue: $113.2 billion, vs. $103.1 billion expectedHigh profits from the largest oil companies at a time of war is politically controversial. President Donald Trump said in August that Chevron and Exxon "were making too much money based on a shortage." The supply disruption began in March after the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran. Profits from Chevron's refining division surged more than 300% to $4.9 billion compared to $1.1 billion in the same period in 2025. Its oil and gas production generated earnings of $5.7 billion, up 70% from $3.3 billion in the year-ago period. watch nowChevron's U.S. refineries processed record amounts of crude oil at just above 1 million barrels per day, as the facilities ran at 98% capacity. Diesel and jet fuel yields rose more than 10%, Wirth said.  Exxon's refining division generated profits of about $7.2 billion in the quarter, outpacing its production business' earnings of about $7.1 billion. Its refining profits have surged nearly 200% to $11.4 billion so far this year compared to $4 billion during the first nine months of 2025. Exxon's Gulf Coast refineries operated at 100% capacity utilization. Those refineries produced "record volumes of diesel" in the quarter, Woods said.Chevron's oil and gas production actually declined slightly to 3.9 million barrels per day compared to about 4 million bpd in the same period last year. The decline was in its international segment due in part to the conflict in the Middle East, while output was largely flat in the U.S. year over year.Exxon has produced about 4.5 million bpd this year, a more than 2% decline from nearly 4.7 million during the first nine months of 2025.

schema.headline: Chevron and Exxon hit all-time highs as refining profits soar in reaction to Iran and Ukraine wars

title: Tankers defy sharp escalation of Iranian attacks to keep crude oil flowing through Strait of Hormuz
description: watch nowWithin 24 hours of the U.S. and Israel going to war with Iran, Tehran responded with a wave of attacks on commercial ships in the Strait of H
body: watch nowWithin 24 hours of the U.S. and Israel going to war with Iran, Tehran responded with a wave of attacks on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz to cut off one of the world's main sources of crude oil. Iran's campaign was initially successful, with crude exports plunging nearly 90% to 1.8 million barrels a day in March compared with 16 million bpd in February, according to data provided by Kpler. But crude flows have rebounded over the past eight months as the U.S. military provides protection to tankers transiting Hormuz. Tehran has responded by escalating its attacks in recent weeks. More commercial ships have come under attack in October than at any other point in the war. Yet in contrast to March when exports cratered, tankers have continued to ferry substantial volumes of crude oil through Hormuz in a sign that the shipping industry has adapted to wartime in the Persian Gulf.As of Oct. 27, at least 30 vessels, mostly oil tankers, were hit this month leaving at minimum 16 seafarers injured, according to data from the International Maritime Organization, a United Nations agency. Ship attacks doubled in October compared with 15 confirmed incidents in September."It's a difficult situation. Ships are attacked really on a daily basis," said Jakob Larsen, chief safety and security officer at Denmark-headquartered BIMCO, one of the big international shipping trade associations. Ship attacks in the Strait of Hormuz surged in OctoberKplerOil prices rise, but flows are resilientCrude prices have surged more than 13% this month as security conditions have deteriorated in the Persian Gulf. The international Brent contract traded above $117 a barrel on Friday. That's just shy of its wartime closing high of $118.35 during Iran's big wave of ship attacks in March. Yet actual crude exports through Hormuz stood at nearly 11.1 million bpd on average in October, only about 2% lower from September despite the sharp escalation of violence, Kpler's data shows. "On balance in terms of oil coming out, there hasn't been a massive impact," said Mary Melton, senior tanker analyst at Braemar, headquartered in London. Crude flows through Hormuz are highly volatile on a daily basis with exports near prewar levels one day while falling well below such levels another day. The final leg of October has seen flows decline to 7.3 million bpd for the week ended Wednesday, more than 40% below the prewar baseline, according to Kpler.Oil flows are more resilient now because the shipping industry has adjusted its operations to the threats, Larsen said. Freight rates have soared, making it "more attractive for the risk takers in the industry to actually carry out these voyages," he said. "And when the cost of oil goes up that also means that there's more commercial incentives to get the oil out and sell it in the global market," Larsen said. Adapting to more perilous timesShippers have adapted by setting up a shuttle system to reduce the risk of attack. Tankers load crude at Persian Gulf ports, sail through Hormuz with their transponders turned off and transfer the cargo to tankers waiting in the Gulf of Oman that then deliver it to refiners in Asia. This reduces insurance costs for the ships waiting outside the strait, Melton said. The shuttle system has been effective at getting oil out with flows through Hormuz surging more than 70% since July, according to Kpler. But this system is also inefficient, logistically complicated and expensive, Melton said. It requires more equipment, ships and experienced crews, the analyst said. About 20% of the world's supertanker fleet is tied up helping to shuttle oil out of the Gulf, she said. Tanker rates have exploded as a consequence. It cost $249,000 per day to hire a supertanker to make the journey from the Gulf of Oman to Asia in early September, Melton said. By the first week of October, the price had surged to $931,000 per day. This translates to about $21 in transportation costs per barrel of crude oil compared with $6.50 a barrel in September, the analyst said."If you're an importer in Asia, you're used to paying almost nothing for freight," Melton said. "Then you're facing 20% to 30% of the actual delivered cost of crude is going to freight."That really starts impacting your margins as a refiner," the analyst said. More Gulf oil producers are now covering the freight costs in a bid to claw back market share in Asia from the U.S., she said. They are also increasingly using their own tankers to run the gauntlet through Hormuz, she said.Uncertainty as midterms approachIt is unclear how long the complex and expensive shuttle system can sustain current export levels. The tankers transiting Hormuz are totally dependent on air support from the U.S. military for their security, Larsen said. "I don't think there would be many shipowners willing to take the risk if they didn't have that air cover from U.S. fighter jets and helicopters and drones," he said.  It is also uncertain how long the U.S. military will remain engaged, particularly if Democrats regain control of Congress after Tuesday's elections and demand that the president end the war. The U.S. has told several Gulf Arab nations to be ready for a short but intense military campaign following the Nov. 3 midterm elections, people briefed on the conversations told The Wall Street Journal. The U.S. Navy, which is enforcing a blockade against Iran, has warned ships that don't need to transit the Persian Gulf, Hormuz and Gulf of Oman to steer clear of the region."Due to the current geopolitical situation, vessels which do not need to transit the area are advised to remain well clear to avoid unnecessary delays to their voyage," the U.S. military told vessels Wednesday through a notice issued by the Joint Maritime Information Center.

schema.headline: Tankers defy sharp escalation of Iranian attacks to keep crude oil flowing through Strait of Hormuz

title: Halloween gets pricier as chocolate costs climb — Hershey may feel the pinch
description: Halloween candy is displayed at a Target store on Oct. 27, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. Justin Sullivan | Getty ImagesHalloween shopping got costl
body: Halloween candy is displayed at a Target store on Oct. 27, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. Justin Sullivan | Getty ImagesHalloween shopping got costlier this year as higher prices hit everything from the candy bowl to the pumpkin on your front porch. It's not only rough on consumers, but may also hit companies like Hershey.Americans are expected to spend $13.5 billion on Halloween, up from last year's record $13.1 billion, according to the National Retail Federation. "Consumers continue to make Halloween a spending priority, but they are also approaching the season with affordability in mind," said Allison Zeller, NRF vice president of industry and consumer insights.Inflation is rippling through everything from candy to costumes. Pumpkins are costlier too. The average retail price reached $5.36 this year, up 11% from September 2020, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. Drought reduced yields by roughly 30% to 40% in parts of Texas, a major pumpkin-growing state.Candy and chocolateCandy remains one of the biggest expenses this Halloween and prices increases are running ahead of broader food inflation, though the rate of increase has slowed. Candy and chewing gum prices were up 7.7% in September from a year earlier, according to the latest Consumer Price Index data. The sugar-and-sweets category increased 5.5% over the same period. Adverse weather, including the impact of El Niño, tightened the outlook for sugar supply. Unusually wet conditions disrupted Brazil's sugarcane harvest, while drought and other weather extremes affected production in other major growing regions."As Halloween swiftly approaches, candy stands out in the grocery store as one of the more expensive categories, relative to prices last year," food economist Richard Volpe wrote on LinkedIn. "In past years, this has left me swimming with candy," he added. "As I write this, Halloween is days away and I have a paltry three bags of candy sitting on my desk."Nielsen IQ Early Market data showed Halloween candy sales down 11.7% through September 19. Four weeks later, the decline narrowed to 6.7%, with chocolate at -7.2% and confection at -5.3%, according to the report.Chocolate so far has been the most vulnerable, especially after a disruption in cocoa supply in West Africa, which was hit by poor growing conditions in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana. A potential El Niño and dry Harmattan trade winds could put pressure on the 2026-27 West African cocoa crop.There was some relief in commodity markets after cocoa prices fell sharply from its historic highs, according to David Branch, sector manager at the Wells Fargo Agri-Food Institute.But that drop has yet to translate into cheaper chocolates.Wells Fargo Agri-Food estimates chocolate prices will be about 8% higher than last Halloween, with effective transaction prices rising roughly 5% to 8% after promotions. Much of the chocolate on shelves this Halloween was produced using cocoa bought six to 12 months earlier."The worst of the cocoa crisis has passed, but price relief hasn't reached store shelves yet," Branch told CNBC. "For chocolate manufacturers, the principal 2026 issue is no longer simply cocoa availability. It is the timing mismatch between falling futures, high-cost inventories, retailer negotiations, and consumer elasticity."Halloween chocolate dollar sales were down 7.2% from a year earlier through the nine weeks ended Oct. 17, according to NIQ, with weakness in milk chocolate leading the decline. NIQ estimates Halloween chocolate sales to be down $33.1 million from last year, with milk chocolate accounting for a $34.4 million decline. Dark chocolate, meanwhile, gained $2.3 million. Overall Halloween candy, gum and mint sales were down 6.7%. To help juice sales, retailers are offering discounts — Walmart and Target have flash deals and heavy discounts on items from candy to Halloween costumes. Candy shoppers, meanwhile, appear to be moving toward smaller packages. Small candy packs of nine ounces or less are up 24% in dollar terms and 14% in units, while every larger package size is declining, according to NIQ. Wells Fargo expects shoppers to increasingly favor value packs and alternatives that use less cocoa, including gummies, sour candy, wafers and caramel."Consumers will continue buying candy, but shopping baskets are likely to contain fewer chocolate pieces, more value packs, and a greater share of gummies, sour products, wafers, caramel, and other lower-cocoa alternatives," Branch said.Hershey stock was rising on Friday as consumers ditched AI stocks for safer consumer staples. But analysts see trouble brewing for the candy maker. The company, which reported third quarter results on Thursday, lowered its 2026 organic sales growth forecast to 3% (from 3%-3.5%). That implies "flattish" organic growth in the fourth quarter, according to Jefferies analyst Scott MarksHershey's commentary was "incrementally cautious," he added in a note, saying "consumer and cost pressures" are weighing on the near-term outlook.    "We're looking at areas like in convenience as you see a consumer that's under pressure to give more value and drive pricing through bespoke promotions versus overall price decreases," Hershey CEO Kirk Tanner told analysts on an earnings call.Marks cut his price target on the stock to $170, joining cuts at brokerages such as DA Davidson, BNP Paribas, Bernstein and Deutsche Bank. Consensus estimates for 2027 earnings fell 3.7% to $9.49 a share, according to FactSet.CNBC's Alex Harring contributed to the reporting.

schema.headline: Halloween gets pricier as chocolate costs climb — Hershey may feel the pinch

title: Rivian third-quarter earnings beat estimates as software revenue, R2 deliveries rise
description: Signage outside Rivian's offices in Palo Alto, California, Dec. 10, 2025.Jason Henry | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesRivian Automotive beat Wall Street's th
body: Signage outside Rivian's offices in Palo Alto, California, Dec. 10, 2025.Jason Henry | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesRivian Automotive beat Wall Street's third-quarter earnings expectations as it ramped up production of its new R2 entry-level SUV that the company has promised investors will lead it to profitability.Here's how Rivian performed in the period ended Sept. 30, compared with average estimates compiled by LSEG:Loss per share: 48 cents adjusted vs. loss of 62 cents expectedRevenue: $2.16 billion vs. $1.99 billion expectedShares of Rivian were up roughly 7% during afterhours trading Thursday, after hitting a new 52-week low of $11.38 earlier in the day. The stock closed at $11.45 a share, down 1.9%The electric vehicle maker also revised its 2026 guidance to mark expected improvements in its vehicle deliveries, pre-tax adjusted earnings and capital expenditures.The new guidance calls for a pre-tax adjusted loss of between $1.75 billion and $1.85 billion — a $100 million improvement at the midpoint from its prior guidance — vehicle deliveries of between 67,000 and 70,000 units, up from at least 65,000; and capital expenditures of between $1.4 billion and $1.5 billion, $300 million less at the midpoint.Rivian attributed the improvement in its pre-tax adjusted earnings guidance to better-than-expected revenue related to its sales of regulatory credits, an IEEPA tariff refund receivable in the third quarter and its expected increase in vehicle deliveries.The R2 — the first deliveries of which arrived to customers in June — has become Rivian's best-selling model and was responsible for "much of the gain quarter-over-quarter," the company said. Rivian delivered a record 19,248 units from July through September. The company does not disclose deliveries by vehicle.watch nowThe EV maker remains unprofitable overall but continued to narrow its losses during the quarter. The company reported a net loss attributable to common stockholders of $913 million, compared with a loss of $1.17 billion during the third quarter of 2025.Rivian's gross profit, which is closely monitored by investors, was $176 million during the third quarter, up from $24 million a year earlier. Its adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization was a loss of $435 million, a $167 million improvement from the same period last year.The company reported that its software and services segment continues to grow, generating $605 million in revenue and a gross profit of $256 million, a 42% margin. That compares to its automotive operations, which recorded nearly $1.55 billion in revenue and a gross loss of $80 million.Also on Thursday, Rivian reiterated that it expects the R2, a smaller and less expensive sibling to its current luxury R1S SUV, to have a positive gross margin by the end of the year. CEO RJ Scaringe has said the company needs to scale beyond current R2 production plans of 160,000 units in order to achieve overall profitability."That ramp-up is critical for us getting to positive gross margin on R2 and that ultimately will contribute to positive gross margin for the business," Scaringe told CNBC's Phil LeBeau during an interview Thursday. "We're going to see that through the end of the quarter and the unit economics will continue to grow … into Q1 of next year as well."Rivian on Thursday said its cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments balance was $5.5 billion, up from $5.3 billion to end the second quarter.watch now

schema.headline: Rivian third-quarter earnings beat estimates as software revenue, R2 deliveries rise

title: Binance's $6.3 billion hack: What we know and what comes next
description: watch nowBinance was hacked with an estimated impact of $6.3 billion, raising questions about the recovery of stolen funds and the broader fallout for
body: watch nowBinance was hacked with an estimated impact of $6.3 billion, raising questions about the recovery of stolen funds and the broader fallout for crypto markets. Around $3 billion in cryptocurrency assets have been frozen so far, according to a Binance security update.The exchange pledged to cover all losses, while blockchain investigators linked the attack to North Korea and analysts assessed the potential financial risks.Bitcoin was under pressure on Friday and was trading below $78,000.Can frozen funds be recovered?Freezing cryptocurrency prevents it from being transferred, but recovering the funds requires a separate legal process, according to Ari Redbord, global head of policy at blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs and a former U.S. federal prosecutor and Treasury official. "A freeze stops the money from moving, and recovery follows through legal process," Redbord told CNBC.Redbord said law enforcement typically obtains a court order or seizure warrant before working with stablecoin issuers to release or reissue assets and return them to their rightful owners."Stablecoins are the most recoverable asset class in crypto because the issuer controls the token contract," he said. "Tether and Circle can freeze, burn and reissue, which allows frozen USDT and USDC to be returned to a victim."But recovering bitcoin and ether is more challenging because they have no issuer that can directly freeze the assets. Instead, investigators must trace funds through exchanges and other crypto services where they can potentially be intercepted, added Redbord. Eric Jardine, head of research at blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis, said returning frozen assets requires coordination among law enforcement, exchanges and token issuers."There is no standard recovery timeline. A technical freeze may happen quickly, while returning funds can take months or years," Jardine told CNBC.Jardine added that while bitcoin and ether cannot be frozen by an issuer, they can still be traced and potentially recovered. Investigators can trace the funds on public blockchains and intervene when they reach a cooperating exchange or another centralized platform, he said.Who is behind it?TRM Labs attributed the attack with high confidence to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-sponsored hacking unit, based on on-chain and off-chain intelligence.The FBI previously identified the same group as responsible for the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025, according to the company's insights. TRM Labs said the Binance attack shared characteristics with previous North Korea-linked incidents, including preparations made well before the theft and transaction signatures obtained in advance.The firm estimated that approximately $6.36 billion in digital assets were moved from Binance wallets across 10 blockchains, with most transferred within about 20 minutes.TRM Labs said preparations for the attack began at least 36 hours before the theft, with the attackers using Tornado Cash, a cryptocurrency mixing service, to fund their wallets ahead of the breach.Chainalysis also pointed to North Korea, with co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin saying the firm assessed that the $6.4 billion Binance hack was likely carried out by TraderTraitor, citing links to previous attacks. Does this pose financial risks?The attack does not currently appear to pose a significant solvency risk for Binance, according to Sean Farrell, head of digital asset strategy at Fundstrat Global Advisors."The most important takeaway for markets is that this does not currently appear to create meaningful solvency risk for Binance," Farrell said.Farrell estimated that around $3.3 billion in assets remained unfrozen. Assuming frozen stablecoins are eventually returned, Binance's SAFU emergency fund, worth approximately $1.2 billion, could cover roughly a third of the remaining losses, with the balance coming from the exchange's own funds.Farrell said the key indicators to watch were how quickly Binance resumes withdrawals and whether outflows remain orderly. He added that a shortfall in customer assets could force the exchange to sell reserves, potentially triggering broader selling across crypto markets."I do not think that is the setup we are dealing with, but the key tell will be how quickly withdrawals resume and whether outflows stay orderly," Farrell said.What does the hack mean for crypto security?The Binance hack underscores the need for stronger cybersecurity standards and greater coordination among governments, according to Chris Perkins, head of Franklin Crypto at Franklin Templeton. Speaking to CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia," Perkins said the industry must address cybersecurity challenges to reach its full potential, calling for stronger defenses and policies to hold cybercriminals accountable.watch now"We need to make sure standards are incredibly high, but we have to really focus on the criminals," Perkins said.Perkins called for greater international cooperation to address cybersecurity threats, pointing to regulatory coordination among G20 countries following the global financial crisis as a potential model.He also said AI could help improve cybersecurity by identifying and addressing vulnerabilities, even as the technology is used by both attackers and defenders.

schema.headline: Binance's $6.3 billion hack: What we know and what comes next

title: Starbucks sales miss expectations, but its U.S. turnaround is gaining steam
description: Starbucks on Thursday reported mixed quarterly results as its international cafes underperformed expectations.However, its U.S. turnaround continues t
body: Starbucks on Thursday reported mixed quarterly results as its international cafes underperformed expectations.However, its U.S. turnaround continues to take hold, as its home market topped expectations during the coffee giant's final quarter of fiscal 2026. "We enter fiscal 2027 with momentum, a clear set of priorities and higher ambitions for what Starbucks can become," CEO Brian Niccol said in a video shared on the company's website.Starbucks is ahead of schedule to meet the fiscal 2028 targets laid out at its investor day in January, he said on the company's earnings conference call.For fiscal 2027, Starbucks is projecting adjusted earnings per share in a range of $3.15 to $3.25, above Wall Street's expectations of earnings per share of $3.14. However, its anticipated revenue decline of 1% is weaker than expected; analysts were forecasting net sales growth of 1.4%. Starbucks is projecting North American same-store sales growth of 4% for the fiscal year. The company's earnings and revenue outlook includes an additional week and the effects of the shift in its China business to a joint venture business model. Starbucks is also projecting slight deflation in coffee prices and slowing net new North American cafe openings, which will both weigh on its full-year revenue, according to CFO Cathy Smith.Here's what the company reported for the quarter ended Sept. 27 compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:Earnings per share: 80 cents adjusted vs. 72 cents expectedRevenue: $9.14 billion vs. $9.23 billion expectedStarbucks reported fiscal fourth-quarter net income attributable to the company of $677.2 million, or 59 cents per share, up from $133.1 million, or 12 cents per share, a year earlier.Excluding restructuring and impairment costs and other items, the company reported earnings per share of 80 cents.Net revenue fell 4% to $9.14 billion, reflecting the joint venture deal in China.The company's global same-store sales increased 7.2%, fueled by growth in average ticket, and beating Wall Street estimates of 6%, according to StreetAccount. Transactions grew 1.8% in the quarter.Starbucks' U.S. cafes reported same-store sales growth of 7.7%, topping StreetAccount estimates of a 6.5% increase.Under Niccol's "Back to Starbucks" strategy, the company has focused on improving service, making its cafes more welcoming and sharpening its marketing. The changes have helped to win back customers."Starbucks brand affinity is at near record levels as our menu innovation, marketing and merchandise continue to create moments that drive culture and bring people into our coffee houses," Niccol told analysts.The company said its North American rollout of its fall menu, which includes the iconic pumpkin spice latte, was the company's strongest ever autumn launch day. And matcha is now a $1 billion drink for Starbucks.Outside of North America, the company's international comparable sales ticked up 0.9%, as traffic declines offset an increase to average ticket. That growth fell short of analyst estimates of a 3.2% increase, according to StreetAccount.After its China business transitioned to a joint venture, Starbucks has shifted most of its international business to a licensed model, allowing local operators to take charge. The company is also exploring selling a majority stake in its Japan business, Reuters reported in September.Starbucks opened 303 net new cafes during the quarter. In September, the company announced it would close about 1% of its North American footprint, or about 250 locations, as part of its turnaround.By the end of its fiscal year, across the U.S. and Canada, the company also completed more than 1,700 cafe uplifts, meant to make its stores more welcoming to customers. The company has said locations that receive a makeover, with tweaks like increased seating and softer lighting, see higher transactions in the aftermath.

schema.headline: Starbucks sales miss expectations, but its U.S. turnaround is gaining steam

title: Cheaper cars are selling considerably faster than at the beginning of the year
description: Consumers are concerned about rising fuel prices and affordability — and that could be showing up in how fast the least expensive cars are moving off
body: Consumers are concerned about rising fuel prices and affordability — and that could be showing up in how fast the least expensive cars are moving off dealer lots.From the first quarter to the third, the number of days it took a dealer to sell a vehicle priced between $20,000 and $29,999 dropped 20%, according to data from Edmunds. That pace of selling saw the biggest acceleration of any price segment. Vehicles priced from $30,000 to $39,999 sold about 18% faster, and the number of days it took to sell the next tier — $40,000 to $49,999 — dropped nearly 12%, according to Edmunds. All of those price segments also took fewer days to turn than their more expensive counterparts. The lower-priced tiers took under 60 days to move off lots, with the least expensive ones selling the fastest. Every segment of vehicles above $50,000, meanwhile, took more than 60 days to sell. "If you're a dealer and you have inventory and that price point, you're definitely noticing," said Edmunds'  Director of Insights Ivan Drury. Cheaper vehicles may be selling faster, but they're still hard to find. The average listing price for a new vehicle in September was $49,726, according to Cox Automotive.And, the overall sales numbers for some key segments priced under $40,000 have fallen. This has especially been true for compact cars, which are down roughly 4% since the beginning of 2026, and compact SUVs, down nearly 8% in the same period, according to Cox Automotive. These different data points seem to be moving in opposite directions. On the one hand, cheaper cars are moving faster off dealer lots. On the other, sales of affordable segments are down. There are a few reasons for this, according to analysts who follow the industry. One is that there might not be enough lower-priced vehicles on dealer lots in the first place. "I think there are some supply things going on at that end of the market," said Cox Automotive Deputy Chief Economist Mark Strand. "We have to kind of grade the market on a curve  until we see what's going on with fourth-quarter data." The compact SUV segment, in particular, is suffering from the lack of two popular models.The Toyota RAV4, which is the most popular SUV in the U.S., has been in short supply at many dealerships this year, as the automaker shifts production to its Kentucky factory, Strand said. The company also has shifted the entire lineup to a hybrid powertrain at a time when hybrids have been in exceptionally high demand. The other missing SUV is the Ford Escape, which that automaker discontinued to make way for its upcoming midsize EV pickup truck. The other slow-selling, low-priced segment — compact cars — faces structural inventory challenges, said AutoForecast Solutions Vice President of Global Forecasting Sam Fiorani. "We've seen the disappearance of affordable, compact new vehicles over the last decade," he said. Detroit automakers swapped out their lineups of compact coupes and sedans in favor of small crossover SUVs, which tend to carry slightly higher sticker prices than comparably sized passenger cars.  Currently, there is not a single compact passenger sedan for sale by an American manufacturer. Most on the market are Japanese or Korean, with a few German models, such as the Volkswagen Jetta and the Golf hatchback."You have all these brands that have just abandoned the marketplace," Fiorani said.The smallest American passenger cars are the Ford Mustang, General Motors' Chevrolet Corvette, and the midsize Tesla Model 3 sedan, according to AutoForecast Solutions. The firm classifies both the Mustang and the Corvette as sports cars, and as such they occupy a different niche than compact sedans like the Honda Civic or Toyota Corolla. The Mustang has a starting price of $33,490, the Model 3 starts at $34,990, and the Chevrolet Corvette starts at $71,300. Cars like the Civic, Corolla and Jetta, meanwhile, all start below $25,000. "Compact vehicle buyers are very price-sensitive," Fiorani said. "And so when the price of gas goes up, that eats into their car payment. That means that they can't afford a $500 or $600 a month car payment, and they have to move into the used market."Indeed, the wholesale used prices of compact cars has risen and is up more than nearly any other segment, according to Cox Automotive. Wholesale prices — the prices vehicles sell for at large auctions, like Cox Automotive's Manheim auction — are indicators for prices overall in the fragmented used car market. Along with the rise in prices, auto finance stats show that a historically high number of buyers are stretching to afford cars. Roughly one in four buyers financing their purchases are getting 84-month loans — a record. Nearly three in 10 trade-ins toward new-vehicle purchases carried negative equity in the third quarter, meaning the cars being traded in were worth less than the outstanding balances of the loans on them. Shoppers are often rolling these negative balances into new loans, which pushes up the new payment cost. Automakers have also been more tightly aligning production with demand to avoid discounting vehicles. Incentives on average are about 6.6% of the average transaction price as of October, according to Cox Automotive. Leasing offers a way to get a car with a lower payment, but leasing rates are also down.Vehicle trade-in data suggests that many buyers who are snapping up those fast-selling cheaper vehicles are either first-time buyers or are purchasing supplemental vehicles, Edmunds' Drury said. The subcompact SUV segment is one lower-priced group that has seen sales rise in 2026. That is a segment that attracts a lot of first-time buyers. But this is still a relatively small share of the total car market, Fiorani said. "It's not the mainstream vehicle that Americans want," he said. "It is the vehicle that entry-level buyers need to get to work, to get to school. ... It's people who don't have families yet."Repeat buyers are less likely to want to step down into a compact car or SUV, Drury said."The moment you get into that other vehicle and it's a little bit smaller, it's not as comfortable, it doesn't fit all your stuff, all your kid's equipment for soccer practice, you're done," he said. "You're not giving up 360 cameras, ventilated seats, heated steering wheels, these niceties that you've become accustomed to.  Automakers know that too. Dealers know that."The truly cash-strapped are either snapping up the relatively few low-priced cars on dealer lots, moving to the used market, or holding on to their cars longer. "The people who are trying to buy the smaller vehicles are really hurt by the way the economy is at the moment," Fiorani said. "So those people are trying to move into used vehicles or trying to maintain their current vehicle as long as they can. Automakers should be prepared for a softening in the marketplace."

schema.headline: Cheaper cars are selling considerably faster than at the beginning of the year

title: Swiss central bank posts bumper $23 billion profit thanks to gold, foreign assets
description: The Swiss National Bank (SNB) headquarters in Bern, Switzerland, on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026. Pascal Mora | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe Swiss National
body: The Swiss National Bank (SNB) headquarters in Bern, Switzerland, on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026. Pascal Mora | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe Swiss National Bank said Friday that it made a profit of 19.1 billion Swiss francs ($23.3 billion) on its investments in the third quarter, driven by its gold and foreign currency holdings. It brought the central bank's year-to-date profit up to 44.2 billion francs, the equivalent of around $53.8 billion, raising the prospect of a payout to Swiss federal and local governments at the end of the year. But the overall profit in the third quarter of 2026 marked a year-on-year decline of almost 32%. Profit and loss recorded in the SNB's quarterly accounting updates consists of interest income, dividends, and valuation adjustments resulting from exchange rate movements and market price changes.The Swiss franc rose around 12% against the U.S. dollar in 2025, having been lifted by investors flocking to the safe-haven currency in the wake of U.S. President Donald Trump's tariff announcements.  So far this year, it has lost around 3.6% versus the greenback.  Profit driversIn the third quarter of 2025, the SNB saw a 14.3-billion-franc net gain on gold, compared to a net gain on gold of 7.6 billion francs in the three months to September.The yellow metal saw a record-smashing rally in 2025, with its value surging by around 66% over the course of 2025. But its trajectory has been far more volatile in 2026, and the metal has fallen in value by more than 7% since the start of the year. Profit on the SNB's foreign currency positions, which include investments in international equities, reached 11.6 billion francs, marking a year-on-year decline of around 15%. Most of the SNB's foreign currency reserves are held in financial assets denominated in foreign currencies, as opposed to hard currency holdings. It also has a smaller Swiss franc bond portfolio. At the end of the third quarter, 61% of its foreign currency reserves were allocated to government bonds, including deposits with central banks and the Bank for International Settlements, while 28% were invested in equities and 11% in other bonds. In terms of currency exposure, 39% of the portfolio was denominated in euros and 37% in U.S. dollars. Japanese yen and British pound exposure accounted for 7% and 6%, respectively.The SNB's stocks portfolioThe SNB's large equity portfolio makes it unusual compared to other major central banks like the U.S. Federal Reserve and the Bank of England, which do not typically invest directly in equity markets. However, the SNB is a passive investor, and therefore does not engage in equity selection. Its stock holdings are based on a benchmark index composed of international stock indexes, with its portfolio mostly made up of shares of mid- and large-cap companies in developed markets. Its profits are mostly distributed to Switzerland's federal and local governments, with shareholders receiving a dividend if its equity capital is large enough. If the investments generate a loss, the SNB may be unable to make payouts. Despite the country benefiting from a strong investment performance, however, the SNB's investments are not focused on achieving the highest possible return. "For a conventional company, profits are an important prerequisite for long-term success. The SNB's goal, by contrast, is not to generate profit," it says on its website. "It has another mandate: It must ensure price stability in Switzerland, while taking due account of economic developments.""The monetary policy mandate always has highest priority. The SNB can thus find itself having to take monetary policy decisions that may have a negative impact on its annual result."Unlike many other major central banks, the SNB's monetary policy mandate allows it to use interest rates and exchange rates to achieve price stability, and it will use measures to influence the exchange rate if deemed necessary. The SNB's inflation target also makes it an outlier among its international peers, with its target range for inflation being 0% to 2%.

schema.headline: Swiss central bank posts bumper $23 billion profit thanks to gold, foreign assets
